newsitem.title: UK: Hypertension in blacks not detected soon enough.
newsitem.headline: Hypertension in blacks not detected soon enough.

text.p: More and more blacks suffer from high blood pressure and the condition is not being detected as early as it should be, doctors said on Sunday.

At the start of a four-day conference that will debate why blacks are more prone to high blood pressure and what can be done about it, they called for better screening methods and more education about the illness.

"All health professionals should be screening for high blood pressure," Dr Elijah Saunders of the University of Maryland School of Medicine told a symposium ahead of the 12th International Interdisciplinary Conference on Hypertension in Blacks.

Hypertension, or high blood pressure, afflicts nearly twice as many blacks as whites in the United States. About a quarter of all African-Americans have high blood pressure. Few studies have been done on black populations in other Western countries.
The condition can lead to kidney and cardiovascular disease, diabetes and stroke and is a top contributor to death in the Western world. But it can be controlled by medication, diet and exercise.
"This population is unique for the excessive amount of target organ damage," Saunders added.
He and other doctors noted that approximately one-third of all people who are hypertensive were unaware of their condition.
They said African-Americans, who are less likely than whites to receive routine medical check-ups, in particular needed to be educated about ways of preventing high blood pressure.

"We need to have a strategy to more aggresively lower blood pressure in three population groups," said Dr Matthew Weir of the University of Maryland School of Medicine, referring to blacks, diabetics and people with symptoms of kidney disease.
The researchers said blood pressure could be reduced in part through changes in life style and diet such as reducing salt and sodium intake.

But many hypertensive blacks needed to be treated with drugs and possibly with combination drug therapy. "Sixty percent of African American patients overall will require more than one drug," Saunders said.
Dr Gordon Williams of Brigham and Womens' Hospital in Boston said one of the major challenges to doctors was persuading patients to take the medication.
